extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, journalists, and general readers seeking an overview of propaganda techniques, models, and history
extracted.subtask_description: A reference-style inventory of common propaganda techniques, psychological mechanisms, and analytic models used to produce or analyze persuasive messaging. Useful for recognizing, evaluating, or designing propaganda-style appeals and media influence strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slogans
rubrics_metrics.description: A slogan is a brief, striking phrase that may include labeling and stereotyping and functions primarily as an emotional appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although slogans may be enlisted to support reasoned ideas, in practice they tend to act only as emotional appeals. Examples: opponents of the US invasion of Iraq used 'blood for oil'; supporters used 'cut and run'. Nationalist slogan example: 'Brazil, love it or leave it'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to arouse prejudices by labeling the object of the campaign as something the audience fears, hates, loathes, or finds undesirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting may focus on stereotypical traits or anecdotal evidence that are unrepresentative of the whole group. In graphic propaganda this may portray enemies with stereotyped racial features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straw man
rubrics_metrics.description: An informal fallacy based on misrepresentation of an opponent's position: substituting a superficially similar proposition and refuting that instead of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To 'attack a straw man' creates the illusion of having refuted a proposition without addressing the actual argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimonial
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of quotations, in or out of context, exploiting the reputation or role (expert, respected public figure) of the individual giving the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places the official sanction of a respected person or authority on a message to cause the target audience to identify with the authority or accept their opinions as its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third party technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing a premeditated message in the 'mouth of the media' by using seemingly independent sources to deliver an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common PR strategy: hiring journalists, using in-house scientists to present potentially prejudicial findings, creating astroturf or front groups. Foreign governments may use advertising and tourism campaigns (or state-owned airlines and services) to promote favorable sentiments abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought-terminating cliché
rubrics_metrics.description: A commonly used phrase, sometimes passing as folk wisdom, used to quell cognitive dissonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, familiar phrases that stop further questioning or critical thought; used to end debate rather than to resolve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer (association)
rubrics_metrics.description: Also known as association: projecting the positive or negative qualities of one person/entity/object/value onto another to make it more acceptable or to discredit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evokes emotional response and stimulates identification with authority. Often highly visual, using symbols (e.g., swastikas) superimposed over other images (e.g., logos); symbols may be used in place of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting that portion of the truth which is requisite for the propagandist's purpose and presenting it so the recipient does not think they are receiving propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote (Richard Crossman): 'The brilliant propagandist is the man who tells the truth, or that selection of the truth which is requisite for his purpose...' The art is not telling lies but selecting truth(s) and mixing them with what the audience wants to hear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unstated assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique where the propagandist repeatedly assumes or implies an idea that would be less credible if explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The desired idea is planted by making it implicit and repeatedly assumed rather than argued for openly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in the target audience's value system that produce a positive image when attached to a person or issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: peace, happiness, security, wise leadership, freedom, 'The Truth'. Associating religiosity or other valued traits can produce affective benefits; considered part of the Transfer technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social psychology factors in persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion influenced by communicator credibility, expertise, trustworthiness, attractiveness, and recipient factors such as interest; includes elaboration likelihood and heuristic models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The elaboration likelihood model and heuristic models indicate when people rely on superficial cues vs. effortful reasoning. Herbert A. Simon's 'cognitive miser' idea: in mass information societies people often decide quickly and superficially. Use of credibility, expertise, trustworthiness, and attractiveness can increase persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Attribution Error
rubrics_metrics.description: A cognitive bias where people tend to attribute others' misfortune to personal failings and downplay external factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propagandists exploit this bias (e.g., portraying poverty as individual failure rather than systemic) to manipulate audience perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-fulfilling prophecies
rubrics_metrics.description: When people believe what they have been told they are, and their behavior makes that belief come true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda can create identities or expectations that cause people to act in ways that confirm the propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusion of control
rubrics_metrics.description: People's desire to believe they can and should control their lives; used by propagandists who claim the other side is attempting to take away that control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims that opponents (e.g., 'big government' or 'big corporations') are trying to control your life and remove freedoms, used to motivate defensive or oppositional reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role theory (role association)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying an idea as appropriate because it is associated with a socially admired role or identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising uses role figures (e.g., the Marlboro Man) to persuade audiences that a product is part of a desired role or identity; effective at linking products/issues to aspirational roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herman and Chomsky's propaganda model (five filters)
rubrics_metrics.description: A model arguing systemic biases in mass media arise from structural economic causes and five filters determining news: Ownership, Funding, Sourcing, Flak, and Anti-communist ideology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The model views private media as businesses selling audiences to advertisers and relying on government/corporate information. The first three filters (ownership, funding, sourcing) are regarded as most important. Though developed for U.S. media, authors see applicability in other similar economic structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ross' epistemic merit model
rubrics_metrics.description: A model defining propaganda via a Sender-Message-Receiver framework and four conditions necessary for a message to be propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four conditions: (1) propaganda involves the intention to persuade; (2) it is sent on behalf of a sociopolitical institution/organization/cause; (3) the recipient is a socially significant group; (4) propaganda is an epistemic struggle to challenge others' thoughts. Ross argues propaganda is not simply falsehood and emphasizes considering conditions of making and use and 'epistemic defectiveness' rather than mere falsity.
